profiles.meeting_scenario: At Meridian Mutual, a mid-sized insurance company, the engineering organization is planning a six-week pilot for small enhancements to its legacy policy administration platform, specifically address-change and beneficiary-update features. Leadership wants to test a hybrid delivery model that combines Agile sprint execution with traditional V-model verification checkpoints to improve process maturity before an upcoming internal audit and to gather evidence for an internal survey on the approach. The meeting agenda is to define the pilot plan: what counts as the pilot scope, which artifacts and verification activities will be produced, who owns each part, and how the team will compare the pilot against the current development process. The expected outcome is a workable plan for the July enhancement release, including responsibilities, timeline, documentation flow, and the metrics that will be reported afterward.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.expertise: Agile delivery, backlog management, developer workflow design, modernization of legacy application teams
members.background: Priya spent several years leading Scrum teams at a product startup before joining Meridian Mutual to improve delivery speed on enterprise systems without disrupting existing governance.
members.private_state: She wants the hybrid pilot to feel lightweight enough that developers will actually adopt it, and she needs quick, visible progress to convince leadership that added maturity does not have to slow the team down.
hidden_assumptions: In a hybrid model for enhancement work, a requirements baseline happens when the sprint backlog is stabilized for implementation, not when a formal signed specification is completed.

For small enhancements, traceability only needs to cover the changed stories and their acceptance tests; unchanged regression areas can rely on the existing regression suite without new explicit links.
Jira and Xray links are sufficient as pilot evidence because the goal is to prove feasibility, not to recreate the full heavyweight release record.
Cycle time for comparing the pilot should focus on the team's execution window, so external approval wait time should not be counted.

members.name: Daniel Cho
members.expertise: Test governance, V-model verification planning, release assurance, audit-ready SDLC controls
members.background: Daniel has spent fifteen years in enterprise quality and release assurance roles, mostly on regulated systems where formal traceability and evidence packages were essential during audits.
members.private_state: He wants the pilot to improve maturity without creating a precedent that teams can bypass established assurance controls, and he is especially worried about evidence gaps that only become visible at release time.
hidden_assumptions: A requirements baseline is only meaningful once it is versioned and approved in the governed requirements workflow.
If work ships in a named release, even a pilot, traceability obligations apply to the whole release package, including regression coverage and downstream verification evidence.
Verification evidence should live in the approved QA repository and follow the normal structure so that it remains audit-ready later.
Any pilot comparison metric must be directly comparable to historical release data, which means measuring from approved baseline to validation sign-off rather than only active engineering time.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to "baseline the requirements next Tuesday."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the product owner and team will freeze the sprint-ready user stories after backlog refinement so development can begin with a stable working set.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the pilot requirements will be formally versioned and approved as a controlled requirements set for the release before verification planning proceeds.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using familiar process language and both expect some kind of freeze point before work proceeds, so the phrase feels precise enough even though each person imagines a different level of formality and duration.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss preparing "the traceability matrix" for the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a lightweight mapping from the pilot's changed stories to acceptance tests and automated checks, mainly for the enhancement items the team is actively building.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a release-level matrix covering business requirements, design references, code, unit tests, integration tests, system tests, and regression evidence for everything included in the July release package.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A traceability matrix sounds like a single standard artifact, so neither person expects to clarify its exact boundaries; each silently defaults to the level of coverage normal in their own workflow.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to compare "cycle time and defect leakage" with the current process after the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 will judge cycle time from sprint commitment to story completion or demo, and defect leakage as issues discovered after story acceptance during later user testing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 will judge cycle time from approved requirements baseline to validation sign-off, and defect leakage as defects found after formal system testing, including UAT and production escapes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The metric names are standard and leadership already asked for a comparison, so both assume the measurement convention is obvious and already shared somewhere in the organization.

turns.inner_thought: I need this six-week pilot to feel practical for the developers, not like we've bolted a full heavyweight SDLC on top of two small enhancements. If we can show visible progress on address-change and beneficiary-update while still hitting a few V-model checkpoints, leadership will see that maturity doesn't have to mean slowdown.
